extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; general educated audience interested in ethical theory
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the moral worth of human actions according to motives (compassion vs egoism/malice), the permissibility and limits of lying, and the primacy of justice and loving-kindness in ethical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of lies for self-defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Every mendacious word is a wrong, excepting only when the occasion arises of defending oneself against violence or cunning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Falsehood is allowable as the one means of opposing inquisitive or suspicious curiosity and for necessary self-defence (examples: lying to avoid robbery; inventing a pretext to avoid danger). The author cites cases (doctors, magnanimous lies, scriptural examples) where falsehoods can be duties. Anti-pattern: unqualified condemnation of all lies; treat lies used beyond self-defence as wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict restriction on lies to a single defensive purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A falsehood must be rigidly restricted to the single purpose of self-defence; otherwise its use admits of terrible abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: as the law allows carrying weapons for self-defence only, Ethics permits lies only for self-defence and for that one purpose. Warning against broad or habitual use of mendacity; Kant's absolute prohibition is rejected as impractical and dogmatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice requires truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is the primary cardinal virtue and requires truthfulness towards all men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although justice demands truthfulness as a general rule, the text situates this within the larger ethical framework that allows narrowly circumscribed exceptions (see permissibility of lies). Justice is foundational for duties of right (Neminem laede).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral worth determined by motive: compassion vs egoism/malice
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion is the sole non-egoistic stimulus and therefore the only truly moral motive; actions have moral worth only when motivated purely by the desire to relieve another's suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human conduct springs from three fundamental motives: Egoism, Malice, Compassion. If a beneficent action has any other motive (reward, reputation, reciprocity, etc.) it is egoistic and lacks pure moral value. Examples of egoistic motives: hope of reward in this or another world, desire for esteem, expectation of reciprocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loving-kindness (caritas/ἀγάπη) as virtue derived from Compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: Loving-kindness is the positive outcome of Compassion (direct suffering-with), producing the precept 'Omnes, quantum potes, juva' (help all people as far as lies in your power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This virtue impels self-sacrifice in varying degrees (bodily/mental effort, property, freedom, life). It grounds duties of love or 'imperfect duties' in Ethics and is distinct from duties of justice. Its origin is immediate empathy rather than reasoned obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of compassion (cruelty) indicates deepest depravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary absence of compassion, manifesting as cruelty, is the surest sign of the deepest depravity and loathsomeness in a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of heinous cruelty are presented to illustrate how lack of compassion elicits universal moral horror. Use presence/absence of compassion as a primary diagnostic of moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical efficacy as a criterion for moral principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral principles should be judged by their operative power in actual conduct; abstract philosophical or religious rules that lack practical efficacy are weaker motivators than Compassion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophic moral principles (e.g., Kantian duty formulated abstractly) and religious injunctions often fail to restrain action when immediate secular fears (punishment, police, honour) are absent. Therefore assess doctrines by their real-world influence on behavior, not merely by formal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight moral blame by victim's vulnerability and suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: The wrongness of harming someone is morally worse when the victim is in adversity or helpless, since such suffering more loudly calls forth Compassion and blame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's point: it is worse to injure the unlucky than the fortunate. Examples: cheating the poor or appropriating goods of widows and orphans is especially heinous. Moral censure is partly a function of the suffering produced, not merely abstract infringement of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion as the root of both justice and loving-kindness
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion underlies and supports both justice and loving-kindness; a person filled with boundless compassion will injure no one and will help and forgive all he can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence of generalized compassionate concern ('may all living beings be delivered from pain') as an integrative test: if someone lacks compassion they cannot truly be virtuous in either justice or charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of motive required for ethical praise
rubrics_metrics.description: An act of beneficence mixed with ulterior motives (seeking reward, esteem, or reciprocal advantage) lacks pure moral worth and should not be praised as genuinely moral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gospel injunctions (e.g., left hand not knowing what right hand does) and Vedic teachings are cited to show that desire for recompense undermines moral merit. Practical test: if the actor's concern is anything other than simply diminishing the other's suffering, the act is egoistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathic identification as necessary condition for Compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion arises when the barrier between self and other is temporarily broken down so that another's suffering becomes, for the moment, a motive for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identification is described as mysterious and not fully explainable by reason, yet empirically observable (examples: spontaneous aid to strangers, mass philanthropic acts). Recognize the psychological/empathic basis when evaluating motives and actions.
